# Improved Quasi-Polynomial-Time Approximation for Maximum Independent Set

Zhao Song<sup>∗</sup>

October 25, 2026

**Abstract**

We give a deterministic quasi-polynomial-time algorithm for the maximum independent set problem. If an _N_-vertex graph contains an independent set of size 2<sup>-_t_</sup>_N_, where _t_ is an integer with \(1\le t\le\sqrt{logN}/12\), then our algorithm finds an independent set of size 2_<sup>t</sup>_ in time _N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>. This gives an approximation ratio of \(N/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{logN})}\) in time \(N^{O(\sqrt{logN})}\), improving on the approximation ratio \(N/2^{\Omega((logN)^{1/3})}\) obtained by Lovett [Lov26].

A limitation of this form of analysis follows from the integrality gaps of Tulsiani [Tul09]. These gaps imply that a universal guarantee of the form \(\mathrm{Las}_{R(t)}(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\Longrightarrow\alpha(G)\ge 2^t\), at \(2^{o(\sqrt{logNloglogN})}\) levels, cannot hold over a range extending beyond \(t=O(\sqrt{logNloglogN})\). Thus, the exponent 1/2 is the limit of this form of analysis, up to a factor of \(\sqrt{loglogN}\).

## 1 Introduction

An independent set in a graph is a set of vertices containing no edge. Given a graph _G_=(_V,E_) on _N_ vertices, the maximum independent set problem asks for an independent set of largest possible size; this size is denoted by \(\alpha(G)\). An approximation algorithm with ratio _R(N_) must output an independent set of size at least \(\alpha(G)/R(N)\). Taking the complement of a graph exchanges independent sets and cliques, so approximation guarantees and hardness results for maximum clique transfer directly to maximum independent set. The decision version is NP-complete by graph complementation and Karp’s NP-completeness result for clique \[Kar72\].

Classical polynomial-time approximation algorithms for general graphs achieve a modest improvement over the trivial factor _N_. Boppana and Halldórsson \[BH92\] obtained an _O(N/_(log_N_)<sup>2</sup>)- approximation by exploiting the structure of graphs that exclude certain subgraphs. Feige \[Fei04\] improved the approximation ratio to _O(N_(loglog_N_)<sup>2</sup>/(log_N_)<sup>3</sup>). These results show that a polylogarithmic saving over the trivial ratio is possible, but they do not give a saving that is a fixed power of the number of vertices.

The theory of probabilistically checkable proofs provides a framework for proving hardness of approximation \[AS98, ALM<sup>+</sup>98\]. Feige, Goldwasser, Lovász, Safra, and Szegedy \[FGL<sup>+</sup>96\] established a connection between interactive proofs and the hardness of approximating clique. Håstad \[Hås99\] subsequently proved that, for every fixed \(\epsilon>0\), a polynomial-time \(N^{1-\epsilon}\)-approximation would imply NP = ZPP. Zuckerman \[Zuc07\] removed the randomness from this hardness result, proving that achieving the same ratio is NP-hard. Thus, assuming \(\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{NP}\), polynomial time cannot provide a fixed polynomial saving over the trivial approximation ratio.

Quasi-polynomial time allows a finer range of approximation ratios. For every fixed _a\>_0, enumerating all vertex sets of size at most \(k:=\lceil(\mathrm{log}N)^a\rceil\) gives an _O(N/_(log_N)<sup>a</sup>_)-approximation in time _N_<sup>_O_((log_N)<sup>a</sup>_)</sup>. The largest independent set found is a maximum independent set when \(\alpha(G)<k\) and has size _k_ otherwise. On the hardness side, Khot \[Kho01\] proved hardness of approximation within \(N/2^{(\mathrm{log}N)^{1-\gamma}}\), for some absolute constant \(\gamma>0\), assuming that NP has no zero-error randomized quasi-polynomial-time algorithms. Zuckerman \[Zuc07\] obtained the same form of hardness using deterministic quasi-polynomial-time reductions, under the assumption that NP has no deterministic quasi-polynomial-time algorithms. Khot and Ponnuswami \[KP06\] strengthened the hardness factor to \(N/2^{(\mathrm{log}N)^{3/4+\epsilon}}\) for every fixed \(0<\epsilon<1/4\), assuming that NP does not have randomized quasi-polynomial-time algorithms with bounded error. Their theorem is stated for polynomial-time approximation algorithms, but their randomized reduction has quasi-polynomial running time and output size. Composing it with a quasi-polynomial-time approximation algorithm would therefore contradict the same assumption.

Recently, Lovett \[Lov26\] gave a deterministic quasi-polynomial-time algorithm with an approx imation ratio of \(N/2^{\Omega((\mathrm{log}N)^{1/3})}\), improving the polylogarithmic saving obtained by enumeration to a stretched-exponential saving. More precisely, there is an absolute constant _c\>_0 such that, for every integer \(1\le t\le c(\mathrm{log}N)^{1/3}\), given the promise \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\), his algorithm finds an independent set of size at least 2_<sup>t</sup>_ in time _N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>. The resulting approximation algorithm runs in time _N_<sup>_O_((log_N_)<sup>1/3</sup>)</sup>. This leaves a substantial gap between the exponent in the algorithmic guarantee and the exponent in the hardness result of Khot and Ponnuswami \[KP06\].

Semidefinite relaxations provide another perspective on this problem. Lovász’s theta function \[Lov79\] gives a semidefinite upper bound on the independence number, and the hierarchy of Lasserre \[Las01\] strengthens such relaxations by imposing consistency and positivity on higher moments. The power of this hierarchy for independent set is limited by the integrality gaps of Tulsiani \[Tul09\]: even \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N\mathrm{loglog}N})}\) levels can have a gap of \(N/2^{O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N\mathrm{loglog}N})}\). These gaps concern the information supplied by the relaxation and are distinct from hardness results for arbi<tbc>

trary approximation algorithms.

### 1.1 Our result

We state our main result as follows.

**Theorem 1.1** (Informal version of Theorem 4.6)**.** _Let t be an integer with_ \(1\le t\le\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N}/12\)_. If_ \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\)_, then a deterministic algorithm finds an independent set of size at least_ 2_<sup>t</sup> in time N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>_. Consequently,_ \(\alpha(G)\) _can be approximated within a factor_ \(N/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N})}\) _in deterministic time_ \(N^{O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N})}\).

We make quantitative progress on the first open problem posed by Lovett \[Lov26, Section 1.3\], concerning the gap between approximation algorithms and hardness for maximum independent set. We improve the approximation ratio achievable in deterministic quasi-polynomial time from \(N/2^{\Omega((\mathrm{log}N)^{1/3})}\) to \(N/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N})}\).

As a consequence of Tulsiani’s integrality gaps, Proposition 4.8 shows that the range \(t=O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N})\) is optimal, up to a factor \(\sqrt{\mathrm{loglog}N}\), for universal implications from the value of the Lasserre relaxation to the existence of an independent set of size 2_<sup>t</sup>_. This limitation applies to implications of the form specified there, at \(2^{o(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N}\mathrm{loglog}N)}\) levels.

## 2 Technique Overview

### 2.1 Lovett’s Method

For integers \(t,h\ge 1\), we describe Lovett’s argument \[Lov26\] in five steps. Here _d(U_) denotes edge density, and averages over _U_ are taken over independently and uniformly chosen vertices.

#### Step 1: Initialize.

For the structural argument, assume that we are given a pseudo-distribution \(\mu\) with \(\sum_u\mu(u)\ge 2^{-t}N\) and sufficiently many levels. Set the initial threshold and vertex set as follows:

\(\tau_0:=2^{-(t+1)},U_0:=\{u:\mu(u)\ge\tau_0\},|U_0|\ge\tau_0N.\) (1)

The size bound follows from the objective bound and \(\mu(u)\le 1\).

#### Step 2: Increase the marginals.

Let \(\nu\) be the current conditioned pseudo-distribution. Suppose \(\nu(u)\ge\tau\) on _U_ and \(d(U)\ge\delta:=2^{-h}\). Set \(M(u,v):=\nu(u,v)/(\nu(u)\nu(v))-1\) and \(\rho:=\mathrm{Pr}_{u,v\in U}[M(u,v)\ge 1/2]\). Choose the smallest odd \(\ell\ge h+1\), so \(2^{-\ell}\le\delta/2\). Then

\(0\le\mathbb{E}_{u,v\in U}[M(u,v)^\ell]\le-d(U)+2^{-\ell}+\rho\tau^{-\ell}\le-\delta/2+\rho\tau^{-\ell}.\) (2)

The first step follows from Schur positivity; the second step partitions correlations by sign and magnitude; the third step uses \(d(U)\ge\delta\) and \(2^{-\ell}\le\delta/2\). Averaging gives a vertex _v_ and a set _W_ with

\(|W|\ge\frac{\delta}{2}\tau^\ell|U|,\nu_v(u)\ge\frac{3}{2}\nu(u)(u\in W).\) (3)

The size bound follows by rearranging Eq. (2) and averaging. The marginal bound follows from \(\nu_v(u)=\nu(u,v)/\nu(v)\) and \(M(u,v)\ge 1/2\).

### Step 3: Iterate.

The choice of \(\ell\) gives \(\ell\le h+2\). Put _A_:=(_t_+2)(_h_+2). When \(N\ge 2^{3(t+2)^2(h+2)}\), deleting _v_ after each conditioning step yields

\(\tau_i=(3/2)^i\tau_0,|U_i|\ge 2^{-(t+1)-Ai}N.\) (4)

The threshold formula follows by iterating the gain 3/2; the size bound uses Eq. (3), \(\tau_i\ge\tau_0\), and a factor of two to account for deleting _v_. Since \(\tau_i\le 1\), fewer than 2(_t_+1) steps suffice, yielding \(|U|\ge 2^{-O(t^2h)}N\) and \(d(U)\le 2^{-h}\).

### Step 4: Enumerate.

For \(\mu(S)>0\), the candidates are

\(U_S:=\{u\in V\backslash S:\mu_S(u)\ge(3/2)^{|S|}2^{-(t+1)}\},|S|=O(t).\) (5)

An SDP supplies feasible pseudo-marginals whose objective value is at least half the target. This slack is accounted for by replacing _t_ by _t_+1. Enumerating _S_ takes _N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup> time. For small _N_, a singleton suffices for the sparse-set bound.

### Step 5: Extract an independent set.

Set _h=t_+1. For \(t\le c(logN)^{1/3}\), choosing _c_ sufficiently small ensures \(|U|\ge 2^{t+1}\). Greedy extraction gives

\(|I|\ge\frac{|U|}{1+d(U)|U|}=\frac{1}{|U|^{-1}+d(U)}\ge 2^t.\) (6)

The first step is the greedy bound; the second step divides by |_U_|; the third step uses the size and density bounds.

## 2.2 Our Techniques

The main changes to the argument in Section 2.1 occur in Steps 2 and 3: selecting a dyadic correlation scale and charging vertex loss to marginal gain improve the sparse-set exponent from _O(t_<sup>2</sup>_h_) to _O(th_). Step 4 adapts the enumeration to variable thresholds; Steps 1 and 5 are unchanged.

### Step 1: Reuse the initialization.

This step is unchanged: Eq. (1) supplies the initial threshold and set. The same normalized covariance matrix and Schur positivity remain available. Taking high entrywise powers requires no additional SDP levels; only conditioning consumes levels.

### Step 2: Select a dyadic scale using geometric weights.

Instead of the uniform bound \(M(u,v)^\ell\le\tau^{-\ell}\) in Eq. (2), keep track of the contributions from individual dyadic scales. Let \(\rho_j:=Pr_{u,v\in U}[2^j\le M(u,v)<2^{j+1}]\), where \(-1\le j\le\lceil log(1/\tau)\rceil-1\). Choose the smallest odd \(\ell\ge h+2\), so \(2^{-\ell}\le\delta/4\). Then<tbc>

\(\sum_j\rho_j2^{(j+1)\ell}\ge d(U)-2^{-\ell}\ge 3\delta/4.\)

The first step uses the same moment partition and positivity; the second step uses \(d(U)\ge\delta\) and the choice of \(\ell\). Assign weights _w<sub>j</sub>_:=2<sup>-(_j_+2)</sup>, whose sum is less than 1. Some class contributes at least \((3\delta/4)w_j\) to this moment sum. Averaging within that class replaces Eq. (3) by

\(|W|\ge\frac{3\delta}{8}2^{-(j+1)(\ell+1)}|U|,\nu_v(u)\ge(1+2^j)\nu(u)(u\in W).\)

The size bound follows by substituting _w<sub>j</sub>_ and dividing by \(2^{(j+1)\ell}\); the marginal bound follows from the conditioning identity and \(M(u,v)\ge 2^j\). Geometric weights avoid a loss depending on the number of scales.

#### Step 3: Charge vertex loss to marginal gain.

Put \(\Lambda:=h+log(16/3)\), \(c_i:=(j_i+1)(\ell+1)+\Lambda\), and \(K:=2(\ell+1)+2\Lambda=O(h)\). Here _c<sub>i</sub>_ includes the loss from deleting the conditioned vertex. Set \(\tau_{i+1}:=(1+2^{j_i})\tau_i\) and let _m_ be the number of conditioning steps. Lemma 4.2 replaces the fixed cost in Eq. (4) by

\(\sum_{i<m}c_i\le K\sum_{i<m}log(1+2^{j_i})=Klog(\tau_m/\tau_0)\le K(t+1).\)

The first step sums the bounds from Lemma 4.2, the second step uses the threshold product, and the third step uses \(\tau_m\le 1\). For \(N\ge 2^{(2K+1)(t+1)}\), Lemma 4.3 retains at least 2<sup>-(_K_+1)(_t_+1)</sup>_N_ vertices. Every gain is at least 3/2, so sparsity is reached after _O(t_) steps. Lemma 4.5 accounts for the singleton case and the slack in the objective, giving \(|U|\ge 2^{-O(th)}N\).

#### Step 4: Enumerate conditioning sets and thresholds.

The SDP setup and shift \(t\mapsto t+1\) are unchanged. We again require \(\mu(S)>0\). The threshold now depends on the gains, so Eq. (5) is replaced by

\(U_{S,w}:=\{u\in V\backslash S:\mu_S(u)\ge\mu_S(w)\},|S|\le 2t+3,w\in V\backslash S.\)

Choosing a vertex _w_ with minimum marginal in the desired set recovers that set exactly. Enumer ating both _S_ and _w_ preserves the running time _N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup> for _h=O(t_).

#### Step 5: Apply greedy extraction with the improved size bound.

The greedy bound in Eq. (6) is unchanged. With _h=t_+1, the improved size estimate becomes

\(|U|\ge 2^{-O(t^2)}N,d(U)\le 2^{-(t+1)}.\)

The proof of Theorem 4.6 establishes \(|U|\ge 2^{t+1}\) for \(t\le\sqrt{logN}/12\). The resulting independent set has size at least 2_<sup>t</sup>_, giving an approximation ratio of \(N/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{logN})}\) in quasi-polynomial time.

The minimum-degree greedy algorithm returns an independent set whose size is bounded below in terms of the graph’s average degree. This will turn the sparse induced subgraphs constructed later into large independent sets.

**Lemma 3.5** (Greedy)**.** _Let H be a graph on_ \(n\ge 1\) _vertices. Repeat the following until H is empty: pick a vertex v of minimum degree, add it to I, and delete v together with its neighbors. The resulting I is an independent set with_ \(|I|\ge n/(1+2|E(H)|/n)\)_, where H in this bound denotes the original graph._

_Proof._ The set _I_ is independent because the neighbors of each chosen vertex are deleted before the next choice. Let \(\Phi(H):=\sum_{w\in V(H)}1/(deg_H(w)+1)\), and let _N<sub>H</sub>_\[_v_\] denote the closed neighborhood of _v_. Consider one round, which removes _N<sub>H</sub>_\[_v_\] for a vertex _v_ of minimum degree. Every \(w\in N_H[v]\) has \(deg_H(w)\ge deg_H(v)\), so the removed terms of \(\Phi\) sum to at most |_N<sub>H</sub>_\[_v_\]|/(deg_<sub>H</sub>(v_)+1)=1. The degrees of the remaining vertices do not increase, so their contributions do not decrease. Hence \(\Phi\) drops by at most 1 per round. It is 0 at the end, so the number of rounds is at least the initial value \(\Phi(H)\). Since \(x\mapsto 1/(x+1)\) is convex on \([0,\infty)\), Jensen’s inequality gives \(\Phi(H)\ge n/(1+D)\), where \(D:=n^{-1}\sum_{w\in V(H)}deg_H(w)=2|E(H)|/n\) is the average degree of the original graph.

## 4 Proof of the main theorem

We prove Theorem 4.6 by finding a large sparse induced subgraph and applying the greedy algorithm. Section 4.1 establishes a dyadic correlation increment that increases the marginals after conditioning on a vertex. Section 4.2 bounds the logarithmic loss in the number of retained vertices in terms of the logarithmic gain in the marginal threshold. Section 4.3 combines these estimates to obtain a large sparse set after _O(t_) conditioning steps. Section 4.4 constructs a feasible pseudo- distribution with rational entries in time _N_<sup>_O(r_)</sup>. Section 4.5 finds a sparse set deterministically by enumerating conditioning sets and thresholds. Section 4.6 chooses the parameters and applies the greedy algorithm to prove the main theorem and its approximation guarantee. Finally, Section 4.7 applies Tulsiani’s integrality gaps to bound the parameter range in which the underlying implication from the Lasserre value to the independent-set size can hold for every graph.

### 4.1 Dyadic increment

The following lemma shows that conditioning on a suitable vertex increases the marginals on a subset of a dense set. It bounds the size of this subset in terms of the correlation scale.

**Lemma 4.1** (Dyadic increment)**.** _Let_ \(\nu\) _be a level-r pseudo-distribution with_ \(r\ge 2\)_. Let_ \(U\subseteq V\) _be nonempty, and let_ \(\tau,\delta\in(0,1]\) _satisfy_ \(\nu(u)\ge\tau\) _for every_ \(u\in U\) _and_ \(d(U)\ge\delta\)_. Let_ \(\ell\) _be an odd positive integer with_ \(2^{-\ell}\le\delta/4\)_, and let_ \(J:=\lceil log(1/\tau)\rceil\)_. Then there are an integer j with_ \(-1\le j\le J-1\) _and a vertex_ \(v\in U\) _such that_

\(\big|\{u\in U:\nu(u,v)\ge(1+2^j)\nu(u)\nu(v)\}\big|\ge\frac{3\delta}{8}2^{-(j+1)(\ell+1)}|U|.\) (12)

_Proof._ Let _M_ be the normalized covariance matrix from Lemma 3.4. By Lemma 3.2-(b), if \(uv\in E\), then _M(u,v_)=-1. Moreover, for all \(u,v\in U\),

\(M(u,v)\le\frac{min\{\nu(u),\nu(v)\}}{\nu(u)\nu(v)}-1=\frac{1}{max\{\nu(u),\nu(v)\}}-1<\frac{1}{\tau}\le 2^J.\)

The first step follows from the definition of _M_ and Lemma 3.2-(b). The second step rewrites the quotient, the third step uses \(\nu(u),\nu(v)\ge\tau\), and the fourth step follows from the definition of _J_.

For each integer _j_ with \(-1\le j\le J-1\), define<tbc>

\(\rho_j:=\frac{|\{(u,v)\in U\times U:2^j\le M(u,v)<2^{j+1}\}|}{|U|^2}.\)

<tbc>Every pair with \(M(u,v)\ge 1/2\) belongs to exactly one of these classes. Partition the pairs in \(U\times U\) into four groups. Edges contribute exactly -_d(U_)|_U_|<sup>2</sup> to the sum of \(M(u,v)^\ell\), since \(\ell\) is odd. The remaining pairs with _M(u,v)\<_0 make negative contributions. Pairs with \(0\le M(u,v)<1/2\) contribute at most \(2^{-\ell}|U|^2\) in total. Finally, the pairs in class _j_ contribute at most \(\rho_j2^{(j+1)\ell}|U|^2\). Consequently,<tbc>

\(0\le\sum_{u\in U}\sum_{v\in U}M(u,v)^\ell\le\big(-d(U)+2^{-\ell}+\sum_{j=-1}^{J-1}\rho_j2^{(j+1)\ell}\big)|U|^2.\)

<tbc>The first step follows from Lemma 3.4; the second step follows from the preceding partition of the pairs. Rearranging gives<tbc>

\(\sum_{j=-1}^{J-1}\rho_j2^{(j+1)\ell}\ge d(U)-2^{-\ell}\ge\frac{3\delta}{4}.\)

<tbc>The first step rearranges the preceding display, and the second step uses \(d(U)\ge\delta\) and \(2^{-\ell}\le\delta/4\). Assign the weight _w<sub>j</sub>_:=2<sup>-(_j_+2)</sup> to class _j_. These weights satisfy<tbc>

\(\sum_{j=-1}^{J-1}w_j=1-2^{-(J+1)}<1.\)

<tbc>The first step sums a finite geometric series, and the second step uses \(J\ge 0\). Therefore some _j_ satisfies<tbc>

\(\rho_j2^{(j+1)\ell}\ge\frac{3\delta}{4}w_j.\)

<tbc>Otherwise, summing the strict reverse inequalities would contradict the preceding lower bound \(3\delta/4\). Rearranging gives

\(\rho_j\ge\frac{3\delta}{4}2^{-(j+2)}2^{-(j+1)\ell}=\frac{3\delta}{8}2^{-(j+1)(\ell+1)}.\)

The first step divides the preceding lower bound by \(2^{(j+1)\ell}\) and substitutes _w<sub>j</sub>_=2<sup>-(_j_+2)</sup>. The second step collects the powers of 2. The additional loss is determined by the selected scale _j_ and is independent of the number of classes.

The quantity \(\rho_j|U|\) is the average over \(v\in U\) of the number of \(u\in U\) with \(2^j\le M(u,v)<2^{j+1}\). Thus some \(v\in U\) has at least \(\rho_j|U|\) vertices \(u\in U\) with \(M(u,v)\ge 2^j\). For every such vertex,

\(\nu(u,v)=(1+M(u,v))\nu(u)\nu(v)\ge(1+2^j)\nu(u)\nu(v).\)

The first step follows from the definition of _M_, and the second step uses \(M(u,v)\ge 2^j\). Together with the lower bound on \(\rho_j\), this proves Eq. (12).

## 4.2 Cost per bit

The following inequality bounds the logarithmic loss in set size in terms of the logarithmic increase in the marginal threshold. The bound is uniform over all dyadic correlation scales.

**Lemma 4.2** (Cost per bit)**.** _Let_ \(\ell\ge 1\) _be an integer and_ \(\Lambda\ge 0\) _a real number. For every integer_ \(j\ge-1\),<tbc>

\((j+1)\ell+\Lambda\le(2\ell+2\Lambda)log(1+2^j).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ If _j_=-1, the left-hand side is \(\Lambda\), while \(log(3/2)\ge 1/2\) implies that the right-hand side is at least \(\ell+\Lambda\). If _j_=0, the left-hand and right-hand sides are \(\ell+\Lambda\) and \(2\ell+2\Lambda\), respectively. If \(j\ge 1\), then \(log(1+2^j)\ge j\), and

\((j+1)\ell+\Lambda\le 2j\ell+j\Lambda\le j(2\ell+2\Lambda)\le(2\ell+2\Lambda)log(1+2^j).\)

The first step uses \(j+1\le 2j\) and \(\Lambda\le j\Lambda\). The second step uses \(\Lambda\ge 0\), and the third step uses \(log(1+2^j)\ge j\).

## 4.3 Iterated conditioning

Repeated conditioning raises the marginal threshold until the retained set becomes sparse. The next lemma bounds the number of conditioned vertices and the cumulative loss in set size.

**Lemma 4.3** (Iterated conditioning)**.** _Let_ \(t,h\ge 1\) _be integers. Let_ \(\ell\) _be the smallest odd integer with_ \(\ell\ge h+2\)_, and define_<tbc>

\(\Lambda:=h+log\frac{16}{3},K:=2(\ell+1)+2\Lambda.\)

<tbc>_Let_ \(r\ge 2t+3\)_, and let_ \(\mu\) _be a level-r pseudo-distribution satisfying_ \(\sum_{u\in V}\mu(u)\ge 2^{-t}N\)_. Assume_ \(N\ge 2^{(2K+1)(t+1)}\)_. Then there are a set_ \(S\subseteq V\) _with_ \(|S|\le 2t+1\) _and_ \(\mu(S)>0\)_, and a number_ \(\tau\in[2^{-(t+1)},1]\)_, such that_

\(U:=\{u\in V\backslash S:\mu_S(u)\ge\tau\}\)

_satisfies_ \(|U|\ge 2^{-(K+1)(t+1)}N\) _and_ \(d(U)\le 2^{-h}\).

_Proof._ Let \(\delta:=2^{-h}\) and \(\tau_0:=2^{-(t+1)}\). The choice of \(\ell\) gives \(2^{-\ell}\le\delta/4\). We construct sets \(\emptyset=S_0\subseteq S_1\subseteq\cdots\) , thresholds \(\tau_0,\tau_1,\dots\) , and integers \(j_0,j_1,\dots\ge-1\). Write

\(U_i:=\{u\in V\backslash S_i:\mu_{S_i}(u)\ge\tau_i\},c_k:=(j_k+1)(\ell+1)+\Lambda.\)

At each index _i_ reached by the construction, we maintain the following invariants, with empty sums equal to 0 and empty products equal to 1:

(a) |_S<sub>i</sub>_|=_i_ and \(\mu(S_i)>0\).<tbc>

(b) \(\tau_i=\tau_0\prod_{k=0}^{i-1}(1+2^{j_k})\) and \(\tau_i\le 1\).<tbc>

(c) \(|U_i|\ge 2^{-(t+1)-\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}c_k}N\).<tbc>

<tbc>These invariants imply two further facts. First,<tbc>

\(\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}log(1+2^{j_k})=log(\tau_i/\tau_0)\le t+1.\) (13)

<tbc>The first step follows from invariant (b), and the second step uses \(\tau_i\le 1\) and \(\tau_0=2^{-(t+1)}\). Each summand is at least log(3/2)_\>_1/2, so _i\<_2(_t_+1), or equivalently \(i\le 2t+1\). Second,<tbc>

\(\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}c_k\le K\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}log(1+2^{j_k})\le K(t+1).\) (14)

<tbc>The first step applies Lemma 4.2 with \(\ell+1\) in place of \(\ell\), and the second step follows from Eq. (13). Consequently,

\(|U_i|\ge 2^{-(K+1)(t+1)}N.\) (15)

This follows by substituting Eq. (14) into invariant (c). In particular, _U<sub>i</sub>_ is nonempty, since the hypothesis implies \(N\ge 2^{(K+1)(t+1)}\).

_Base case._ Let \(S_0:=\emptyset\). Then \(\mu(S_0)=1\), \(\mu_{S_0}=\mu\), and \(\tau_0\le 1\). Moreover,

\(2^{-t}N\le\sum_{u\in V}\mu(u)\le|U_0|+\tau_0N.\)

The first step follows from the assumed objective bound. The second step uses Lemma 3.2-(a) on _U_<sub>0</sub> and the bound \(\mu(u)<\tau_0\) outside _U_<sub>0</sub>. Hence \(|U_0|\ge 2^{-(t+1)}N\), establishing invariant (c) for _i_=0.

_Inductive Step._ Suppose that the invariants hold at index _i_ and that \(d(U_i)>\delta\). The bound \(i\le 2t+1\) gives \(i\le r-2\), so Lemma 3.3 shows that \(\nu:=\mu_{S_i}\) is a level-(_r-i_) pseudo-distribution with \(r-i\ge 2\). The set _U<sub>i</sub>_ is nonempty by Eq. (15), and every \(u\in U_i\) satisfies \(\nu(u)\ge\tau_i\). Invariant (b) gives \(\tau_i\in[\tau_0,1]\), and therefore \(J:=\lceil log(1/\tau_i)\rceil\le t+1\).

Apply Lemma 4.1 to \(\nu,U_i,\tau_i,\delta,\ell\). It gives an integer _j<sub>i</sub>_ with \(-1\le j_i\le J-1\le t\) and a vertex \(v_i\in U_i\) such that<tbc>

\(W:=\{u\in U_i:\nu(u,v_i)\ge(1+2^{j_i})\nu(u)\nu(v_i)\}\)

<tbc>satisfies

\(|W|\ge\frac{3\delta}{8}2^{-(j_i+1)(\ell+1)}|U_i|=2^{-h-log(8/3)-(j_i+1)(\ell+1)}|U_i|=2^{1-c_i}|U_i|.\)

The first step follows from Eq. (12). The second step uses \(\delta=2^{-h}\), and the third step uses the definitions of \(\Lambda\) and _c<sub>i</sub>_.

Set \(S_{i+1}:=S_i\cup\{v_i\}\) and \(\tau_{i+1}:=(1+2^{j_i})\tau_i\). Since \(v_i\in U_i\subseteq V\backslash S_i\), we have |_S_<sub>_i_+1</sub>|=_i_+1. Since \(\nu(v_i)\ge\tau_i>0\), Lemma 3.3 gives \(\mu(S_{i+1})>0\). Thus invariant (a) holds at the next index.

For \(u\in W\backslash\{v_i\}\), we have \(u\notin S_{i+1}\) and<tbc>

\(\mu_{S_{i+1}}(u)=\frac{\nu(u,v_i)}{\nu(v_i)}\ge(1+2^{j_i})\nu(u)\ge(1+2^{j_i})\tau_i=\tau_{i+1}.\)

<tbc>The first step follows from the conditioning identity in Lemma 3.3. The second step uses \(u\in W\) , the third step uses \(u\in U_i\), and the fourth step follows from the definition of \(\tau_{i+1}\). Thus \(W\backslash\{v_i\}\subseteq U_{i+1}\).

Since \(j_i+1\le t+1\) and \(\ell+1+\Lambda=K/2\),<tbc>

\(c_i\le(t+1)(\ell+1)+\Lambda\le(t+1)K/2.\)

<tbc>The first step uses \(c_i=(j_i+1)(\ell+1)+\Lambda\) and \(j_i+1\le t+1\). The second step uses \(\Lambda\ge 0\), \(t+1\ge 1\), and \(K=2(\ell+1+\Lambda)\). Consequently,<tbc>

\(|W|\ge 2^{1-c_i}|U_i|\ge 2^{1-(t+1)K/2-(K+1)(t+1)}N\ge 2.\)

<tbc>The first step was proved above. The second step uses the bound on _c<sub>i</sub>_ and Eq. (15). The third step uses \(N\ge 2^{(2K+1)(t+1)}\); after substitution, the exponent is \(1+K(t+1)/2\ge 1\). It follows that

\(|U_{i+1}|\ge|W|-1\ge|W|/2\ge 2^{-c_i}|U_i|.\)

The first step uses \(W\backslash\{v_i\}\subseteq U_{i+1}\), the second step uses \(|W|\ge 2\), and the third step uses \(|W|\ge 2^{1-c_i}|U_i|\). Together with invariant (c) at index _i_, this establishes invariant (c) at index _i_+1.

The product formula in invariant (b) follows from the definition of \(\tau_{i+1}\). Also, _W_\\{_v<sub>i</sub>_} is nonempty. For any _u_ in this set, the preceding conditioning bound gives \(\tau_{i+1}\le\mu_{S_{i+1}}(u)\), while Lemma 3.2-(a) gives \(\mu_{S_{i+1}}(u)\le 1\). The latter bound applies because \(\mu_{S_{i+1}}\) is a level-(_r-i_-1) pseudo-distribution and \(r-i-1\ge 1\). This establishes invariant (b) at the next index.

_Termination._ Each step adds at least log(3/2) to the sum in Eq. (13), while that sum is at most _t_+1. The construction must therefore reach an index _i_<sub>∗</sub> with \(d(U_{i_*})\le\delta\). Take _S_:=_S_<sub>_i_<sub>∗</sub></sub> and \(\tau:=\tau_{i_*}\). Invariant (a) and the bound \(i_*\le 2t+1\) establish the required properties of _S_. Invariant (b) gives \(\tau\in[2^{-(t+1)},1]\), and Eq. (15) gives the required size bound.

## 4.4 Computing a pseudo-distribution

The next lemma computes a feasible pseudo-distribution whose total marginal mass is at least half the promised lower bound on the independent-set size. Its rational entries allow the subsequent enumeration and threshold comparisons to use exact arithmetic.

**Lemma 4.4** (Computing a pseudo-distribution)**.** _Let_ \(r,t\ge 1\) _be integers with_ \(N\ge 2^t\)_. There is a deterministic algorithm running in time N_<sup>_O(r_)</sup> _that outputs a level-r pseudo-distribution_ \(\mu\) _with rational values. If_ \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\)_, then the output satisfies_ \(\sum_{u\in V}\mu(u)\ge 2^{-(t+1)}N\).

_Proof._ Let I_<sub>k</sub>_ be the family of independent sets of size at most _k_, and write \(n_k:=|\mathcal{I}_k|\le(N+1)^k\). Consider vectors \(y=(y_T)_{T\in\mathcal{I}_{2r}}\) with \(y_\emptyset=1\). Define \(\mu_y(T):=y_T\) for \(T\in\mathcal{I}_{2r}\), and \(\mu_y(T):=0\) for \(T\in\mathcal{V}_{2r}\) containing an edge. Let

\(M(y):=(m_{A,B})_{A,B\in\mathcal{I}_r},m_{A,B}:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
y_{A\cup B}, & \text{if}A\cup B\text{is independent}, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{array}\right.\)

This is well defined because \(|A\cup B|\le 2r\).

_Claim 1:_ \(\mu_y\) _is a level-r pseudo-distribution if and only if_ \(M(y)\unknown 0\). The conditions in Definition 3.1-(a) and Definition 3.1-(b) hold by construction. If \(A\in\mathcal{V}_r\) contains an edge, then \(A\cup B\) contains an edge for every _B_, so the row of \(M_r[\mu_y]\) indexed by _A_ is zero. Hence \(M_r[\mu_y]\) is positive semidefinite if and only if its principal submatrix on I_<sub>r</sub>_, which is _M(y_), is positive semidefinite.

Let<tbc>

\(F:=\{y:y_\emptyset=1,M(y)\unknown 0\},f(y):=\sum_{u\in V}y_{\{u\}},\text{OPT}:=max_{y\in F}f(y).\)

The set _F_ is convex and closed.

_Claim 2: every_ \(y\in F\) _satisfies_ \(|y_T|\le 1\) _for all T; in particular,_ \(\mathrm{OPT}\le N\). For \(A\in\mathcal{I}_r\), the principal submatrix on the indices \(\emptyset,A\) gives \(0\le y_A\le 1\), as in Lemma 3.2-(a). For \(T\in\mathcal{I}_{2r}\), partition \(T=A\cup B\) into disjoint independent sets with \(|A|,|B|\le r\). The corresponding \(2\times 2\) submatrix has entries _y<sub>A</sub>,y<sub>T</sub>,y<sub>B</sub>_, so positive semidefiniteness gives \(y_T^2\le y_Ay_B\). The bounds on _y<sub>A</sub>_ and _y<sub>B</sub>_ give \(y_Ay_B\le 1\). Thus _F_ is bounded, and its closedness ensures that the maximum defining OPT is attained.

_Claim 3:_ \(\mathrm{OPT}\ge\alpha(G)\). Let _I_<sub>∗</sub> be a maximum independent set, and set \(y_T^*:=\mathbf{1}[T\subseteq I_*]\). For \(A\in\mathcal{I}_r\), define \(\chi_A:=\mathbf{1}[A\subseteq I_*]\). Then \(M(y^*)=\chi\chi^\top\unknown 0\). The first step follows from \(\mathbf{1}[A\cup B\subseteq I_*]=\chi_A\chi_B\), with both sides zero whenever \(A\cup B\) is not independent. The second step follows because an outer product is positive semidefinite. Moreover, _f(y_<sup>∗</sup>)=|_I_<sub>∗</sub>|, which proves the claim.

_Claim 4: the point_ \(y_T^0:=|\{I\in\mathcal{I}_r:T\subseteq I\}|/n_r\) _satisfies_ \(y^0\in F\) _and_ \(M(y^0)\unknown\widehat{\lambda}\mathrm{Id}\)_, where_ \(\widehat{\lambda}:=n_r^{-3}\). Let \(X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{I}_r\times\mathcal{I}_r}\) have entries \(X(A,I):=\mathbf{1}[A\subseteq I]\). Then<tbc>

\((XX^\top)(A,B)=|\{I\in\mathcal{I}_r:A\cup B\subseteq I\}|.\)

<tbc>The equality follows by expanding the matrix product: each summand is 1 exactly when \(A\cup B\subseteq I\). This entry is zero if \(A\cup B\) is not independent, so \(M(y^0)=XX^\top/n_r\). The inverse of _X_ is given by<tbc>

\(X^{-1}(I,B)=(-1)^{|B|-|I|}\mathbf{1}[I\subseteq B].\)

<tbc>Indeed,<tbc>

\(\sum_{I\in\mathcal{I}_r}X(A,I)X^{-1}(I,B)=\sum_{I:A\subseteq I\subseteq B}(-1)^{|B|-|I|}=\mathbf{1}[A=B].\)

<tbc>The first step follows from the definitions; every subset of \(B\in\mathcal{I}_r\) belongs to I_<sub>r</sub>_. The second step follows from the binomial identity, with an empty sum when \(A\unknown\subseteq B\). Since every entry of _X_<sup>-1</sup> lies in {0,1,-1},<tbc>

\(\|X^{-1}\|_\mathrm{op}\le\|X^{-1}\|_\mathrm{F}\le n_r.\)

<tbc>The first step compares the operator and Frobenius norms, and the second step bounds the sum of the squares of the \(n_r^2\) entries. Consequently,

\(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(M(y^0))=n_r^{-1}\|X^{-1}\|_\mathrm{op}^{-2}\ge n_r^{-3}=\widehat{\lambda}.\)

The first step uses \(M(y^0)=XX^\top/n_r\) and the singular values of _X_. The second step uses the preceding norm bound, and the third step uses the definition of \(\widehat{\lambda}\). This proves Claim 4.

_Claim 5:_ \(M(y)-M(y')\unknown-n_r\|y-y'\|_2\mathrm{Id}\) _for all_ \(y,y'\). The map \(z\mapsto M(y+z)-M(y)\) is linear, and each entry of the resulting matrix is either zero or a coordinate of _z_. Therefore

\(\|M(y+z)-M(y)\|_\mathrm{op}\le\|M(y+z)-M(y)\|_\mathrm{F}\le n_r\|z\|_\infty\le n_r\|z\|_2.\)

The first step compares the operator and Frobenius norms, the second step bounds the \(n_r^2\) entries, and the third step compares vector norms. The lower bound on the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix proves Claim 5.

Use the coordinates \((y_T)_{T\neq\emptyset}\), so that the affine constraint \(y_\emptyset=1\) is imposed implicitly. By Claims 2, 4, and 5, _F_ is a well-bounded, full-dimensional convex body in dimension _D_:=_n_<sub>2_r_</sub>-1. It contains the ball of radius \(\rho_0:=\widehat{\lambda}/n_r\) centered at _y_<sup>0</sup> and is contained in the ball of radius \(2\sqrt{D}\) centered at _y_<sup>0</sup>.

A separation oracle for _F_ can be implemented in polynomial time using exact rational arithmetic. Symmetric Gaussian elimination on _M(y_) either certifies positive semidefiniteness or produces a rational vector _x_ with \(x^\top M(y)x<0\). In the latter case, write the affine function \(x^\top M(z)x\) in the reduced coordinates as \(a^\top z+b\). Every \(z\in F\) satisfies \(a^\top z+b\ge 0\), while \(a^\top y+b<0\), so \(a^\top z\ge-b\) is a separating inequality.

For \(\epsilon>0\), let \(S(F,\epsilon)\) be the set of points at Euclidean distance at most \(\epsilon\) from _F_, and let \(S(F,-\epsilon)\) be the set of points whose closed \(\epsilon\)-ball lies in _F_. By the ellipsoid method for weak optimization over a well-bounded convex body with a separation oracle \[GLS88, Chapter 4\], for every rational \(\epsilon\in(0,\rho_0)\) one can compute a rational \(y^1\in S(F,\epsilon)\) such that

\(f(y^1)\ge f(x)-\epsilon\text{for every}x\in S(F,-\epsilon).\)

The running time is polynomial in _D_, \(log(1/\rho_0)\), \(log(1/\epsilon)\), and the encoding lengths of the rational data.

We next express this guarantee in terms of OPT. Fix a rational \(\eta\in(0,1)\), choose \(x^*\in F\) with _f(x_<sup>∗</sup>)=OPT, and set<tbc>

\(\epsilon:=\frac{\eta\rho_0}{2N},\lambda:=\frac{\epsilon}{\rho_0}=\frac{\eta}{2N},x':=(1-\lambda)x^*+\lambda y^0.\)

<tbc>The identity \(\lambda=\eta/(2N)\) follows by substituting the definition of \(\epsilon\). For every _z_ with \(\|z\|_2\le\epsilon\), the point \(y^0+z/\lambda\) belongs to the ball of radius \(\rho_0\) around _y_<sup>0</sup>, hence to _F_. Convexity then gives \(x'+z=(1-\lambda)x^*+\lambda(y^0+z/\lambda)\in F\). Thus \(x'\in S(F,-\epsilon)\). Moreover,<tbc>

\(f(x')\ge(1-\lambda)\text{OPT}\ge\text{OPT}-\eta/2.\)

<tbc>The first step uses \(f(y^0)\ge 0\), and the second step uses \(\text{OPT}\le N\) and \(\lambda=\eta/(2N)\). The weak optimization guarantee now gives

\(\text{dist}(y^1,F)\le\epsilon\le\eta,f(y^1)\ge f(x')-\epsilon\ge\text{OPT}-\eta.\)

In the distance bound, the first step follows from \(y^1\in S(F,\epsilon)\) and the second step uses \(\epsilon\le\eta/2\). In the objective bound, the first step follows from weak optimization and the second step uses the preceding bound on \(f(x')\) and \(\epsilon\le\eta/2\). The inequality \(\epsilon\le\eta/2\) follows from \(\rho_0\le 1\le N\).

Take \(\eta:=\widehat{\lambda}/(4Nn_r)\) and \(\eta':=\eta n_r=\widehat{\lambda}/(4N)\). Applying Claim 5 to _y_<sup>1</sup> and a nearest point in the compact set _F_ gives \(M(y^1)\unknown-\eta'\text{Id}\). Define<tbc>

\(\theta:=\frac{\eta'}{\eta'+\widehat{\lambda}}=\frac{1}{4N+1},y:=(1-\theta)y^1+\theta y^0,\)

<tbc>and output \(\mu:=\mu_y\). The identity \(\theta=1/(4N+1)\) follows by substituting \(\eta'=\widehat{\lambda}/(4N)\) into the definition of \(\theta\). The vector _y_ is rational and has \(y_\emptyset=1\). Also,<tbc>

\(M(y)=(1-\theta)M(y^1)+\theta M(y^0)\unknown\big(\theta\widehat{\lambda}-(1-\theta)\eta'\big)\text{Id}=0.\)

<tbc>The first step uses that _M_ is affine in the reduced coordinates and the coefficients sum to one. The second step combines Claim 4 with \(M(y^1)\unknown-\eta'\text{Id}\), and the third step follows from the definition of \(\theta\). Thus Claim 1 shows that \(\mu\) is a level-_r_ pseudo-distribution. Finally,<tbc>

\(f(y)\ge(1-\theta)(\text{OPT}-\eta)\ge\text{OPT}-\eta-\theta\text{OPT}\ge\text{OPT}-\frac{1}{2}.\)

The first step uses \(f(y^0)\ge 0\) and \(f(y^1)\ge\mathrm{OPT}-\eta\). The second step discards the nonnegative term \(\theta\eta\), and the third step uses \(\eta\le 1/4\), \(\theta\le 1/(4N)\), and \(\mathrm{OPT}\le N\). If \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\), then

\(f(y)\ge 2^{-t}N-\frac{1}{2}\ge 2^{-(t+1)}N.\)

The first step combines Claim 3 with the preceding objective guarantee, and the second step uses \(N\ge 2^t\).

For the running time, \(D\le(N+1)^{2r}\), and \(\mathrm{log}(1/\rho_0)\), \(\mathrm{log}(1/\eta)\), and \(\mathrm{log}(1/\epsilon)\) are all _O(r_log_N_). Computing _y_<sup>0</sup> requires only enumeration of I_<sub>r</sub>_ and its subsets. All rational operations above have bit complexity polynomial in these parameters. The total running time is therefore _N_<sup>_O(r_)</sup>.

## 4.5 Finding a large sparse set

The following lemma converts the conditioning result into a deterministic algorithm by enumerating small conditioning sets and marginal thresholds. The algorithm produces a sparse induced subgraph of the required size.

**Lemma 4.5** (Finding a large sparse set)**.** _Let_ \(t,h\ge 1\) _be integers. Let_ \(\ell\) _be the smallest odd integer with_ \(\ell\ge h+2\)_, and define_<tbc>

\(\Lambda':=h+\mathrm{log}\frac{16}{3},K':=2(\ell+1)+2\Lambda'.\)

<tbc>_If_ \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\)_, then a deterministic algorithm running in time N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>+_O_(log(_h_+1)) _finds a nonempty_ \(U\subseteq V\) _such that_

\(|U|\ge 2^{-(2K^\prime+1)(t+2)}N,d(U)\le 2^{-h}.\) (16)

_In particular,_ \(|U|\ge 2^{-O(th)}N\)_. The additive term accounts for reading the binary parameter h; when h=O(t_) _it is absorbed in N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>.

_Proof._ If \(N<2^{(2K^\prime+1)(t+2)}\), output a single vertex. Its density is zero, and its size satisfies Eq. (16).

Otherwise, \(N\ge 2^t\). Let _r_:=2_t_+5, and compute \(\mu\) using Lemma 4.4. The hypothesis on \(\alpha(G)\) gives \(\sum_{u\in V}\mu(u)\ge 2^{-(t+1)}N\). Apply Lemma 4.3 with _t_+1 in place of _t_. Its constants are \(\Lambda'\) and \(K'\), and its hypotheses hold because _r_=2(_t_+1)+3 and \(N\ge 2^{(2K^\prime+1)(t+2)}\). It gives _S_ with \(|S|\le 2t+3\) and \(\mu(S)>0\), and \(\tau\in[2^{-(t+2)},1]\), for which

\(U_*:=\{u\in V\backslash S:\mu_S(u)\ge\tau\}\)

satisfies \(|U_*|\ge 2^{-(K^\prime+1)(t+2)}N\) and \(d(U_*)\le 2^{-h}\).

To find _S_ and \(\tau\), the algorithm enumerates every \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|\le 2t+3\) and \(\mu(S)>0\), and every \(w\in V\backslash S\). For each pair, it computes

\(U_{S,w}:=\{u\in V\backslash S:\mu_S(u)\ge\mu_S(w)\}.\)

It outputs the first candidate with \(|U_{S,w}|\ge 2^{-(K^\prime+1)(t+2)}N\) and \(d(U_{S,w})\le 2^{-h}\); if there is no such candidate, it reports failure. Under the lemma’s hypothesis, a suitable candidate exists: take _S_ from Lemma 4.3 and choose _w_ minimizing \(\mu_S\) over the nonempty set _U_<sub>∗</sub>. Every \(u\in U_*\) has \(\mu_S(u)\ge\mu_S(w)\). Conversely, if \(u\in V\backslash S\) has \(\mu_S(u)\ge\mu_S(w)\), then \(\mu_S(u)\ge\tau\), because \(w\in U_*\). Thus _U<sub>S,w</sub>=U_<sub>∗</sub>. Its size bound implies the weaker bound in Eq. (16).

Each value \(\mu_S(u)=\mu(S\cup\{u\})/\mu(S)\) is available because \(|S\cup\{u\}|\le 2t+4\le 2r\). The first step uses \(|S|\le 2t+3\), and the second step uses _r_=2_t_+5. There are at most (_N_+1)<sup>2_t_+4</sup> pairs, and each requires poly(_N_) arithmetic operations on rationals of bit length _N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>.

To implement the size tests exactly, use \(2^{K^\prime}=2^{2\ell+2h+10}/9\), which is rational, as are both powers of 2 used in the size tests. No approximation of a logarithm is required. To handle arbitrarily large values of _h_ given in binary, first check whether \(h\ge\lceil\mathrm{log}N\rceil\). In that case \((2K'+1)(t+2)>\mathrm{log}N\), so a singleton already satisfies Eq. (16). Otherwise \(h<\lceil\mathrm{log}N\rceil\), and all powers needed in the tests have bit length polynomial in _t_ and log_N_. Together with Lemma 4.4, this proves the running-time bound. Finally, \(\ell\le h+3\) and log(16/3)_\<_5/2 give \(K'\le 4h+13\), so the exponent in Eq. (16) is _O(th_) for \(t,h\ge 1\).

## 4.6 Completing the proof of the main theorem

We now combine the sparse-set bound with the greedy algorithm to prove the main theorem.

**Theorem 4.6** (Formal version of Theorem 1.1)**.** _Let G be a graph on N vertices, and let t be an integer with_ \(1\le t\le\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N}/12\)_. If_ \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\)_, then a deterministic algorithm finds an independent set of size at least_ 2_<sup>t</sup> in time N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>_. Consequently, a deterministic algorithm running in time_ \(N^{O(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N})}\) _outputs an independent set of size at least_ \(\alpha(G)2^T/N\)_, where_ \(T:=\lfloor\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N}/12\rfloor\).

_Proof._ Apply Lemma 4.5 with _h_:=_t_+1. Then \(\ell\le h+3=t+4\). Since log(16/3)_\<_5/2,<tbc>

\(\Lambda'=h+\mathrm{log}\frac{16}{3}\le t+\frac{7}{2}.\)

<tbc>The first step uses the definition of \(\Lambda'\), and the second step uses _h=t_+1 and the preceding logarithm bound. Therefore<tbc>

\(K'=2(\ell+1)+2\Lambda'\le 4t+17.\)

<tbc>The first step uses the definition of \(K'\), and the second step substitutes the bounds on \(\ell\) and \(\Lambda'\). It follows that

\((2K'+1)(t+2)\le(8t+35)(t+2)\le 43t\cdot 3t=129t^2.\)

The first step uses \(K'\le 4t+17\). The second step uses \(8t+35\le 43t\) and \(t+2\le 3t\), which follow from \(t\ge 1\). The third step multiplies the constants. By Eq. (16), the output _U_ therefore satisfies \(|U|\ge 2^{-129t^2}N\) and \(d(U)\le 2^{-(t+1)}\).

The restriction on _t_ gives \(144t^2\le\mathrm{log}N\). Also \(t+1\le 2t^2\) for integers \(t\ge 1\), so

\(129t^2+t+1\le 131t^2\le\mathrm{log}N.\)

The first step uses \(t+1\le 2t^2\), and the second step uses \(131\le 144\) and \(144t^2\le\mathrm{log}N\). Consequently \(|U|\ge 2^{t+1}\).

Run the greedy algorithm of Lemma 3.5 on _G_\[_U_\]. Since 2|_E(G_\[_U_\])|/|_U_|=_d(U_)|_U_|, it returns an independent set of _G_ with size at least

\(\frac{|U|}{1+d(U)|U|}=\frac{1}{|U|^{-1}+d(U)}\ge\frac{1}{2^{-(t+1)}+2^{-(t+1)}}=2^t.\)

The first step divides numerator and denominator by |_U_|. The second step uses \(|U|\ge 2^{t+1}\) and \(d(U)\le 2^{-(t+1)}\), and the third step simplifies the denominator. The running time is _N_<sup>_O(t_)</sup>.

For the approximation guarantee, if _T_=0, output any vertex; its size is at least \(\alpha(G)/N\). Otherwise, run the algorithm above with _t_:=_T_. If it returns an independent set of size at least<tbc>

2_<sup>T</sup>_, output it; otherwise output a single vertex. If \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-T}N\), the output has size at least 2_<sup>T</sup>_, which is at least \(\alpha(G)2^T/N\) because \(\alpha(G)\le N\). If \(\alpha(G)<2^{-T}N\), a singleton has size greater than \(\alpha(G)2^T/N\). The algorithm runs in time _N_<sup>_O(T_)</sup> whether or not the promise holds: the SDP computation and the finite enumeration do not depend on the promise, and the enumeration reports failure if it finds no suitable candidate. This establishes the claimed running time \(N^{O(\sqrt{logN})}\).

## 4.7 A Limitation of the Analysis

We use the total singleton mass to measure the value of the relaxation at a given level.

**Definition 4.7** (Lasserre value)**.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be a graph and let_ \(r\ge 1\) _be an integer. The level-r Lasserre value of G is_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Las}_r(G):=\mathrm{max}\{\sum_{u\in V}\mu(u):\mu\text{\textit{is a level-r pseudo-distribution for}}G\}.\)

<tbc>The proof of Theorem 4.6 uses \(\alpha(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\) only through the pseudo-distribution computed in Lemma 4.4. The proof of that lemma approximates Las<sub>2_t_+5</sub>(_G_) from below to additive error 1/2. Thus the same argument proves, for \(1\le t\le\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N}/12\),

\(\mathrm{Las}_{2t+5}(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\Longrightarrow\alpha(G)\ge 2^t.\) (17)

The following consequence of Tulsiani’s integrality-gap theorem limits the parameter range in which this implication can hold for every graph.

**Proposition 4.8** (A limit for implications from the Lasserre value)**.** _There are constants c,C\>_0 _and infinitely many integers_ \(N\ge 4\) _with the following property. Write_<tbc>

\(q_N:=\sqrt{\mathrm{log}N\mathrm{loglog}N},R_N:=\lfloor 2^{cq_N}\rfloor.\)

<tbc>_There exist a graph G on N vertices and an integer T with_ \(1\le T\le Cq_N\) _such that, simultaneously for every integer_ \(1\le r\le R_N\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Las}_r(G)\ge 2^{-T}N\text{\textit{and}}\alpha(G)<2^T.\) (18)

<tbc>_Proof._ By Tulsiani’s integrality-gap theorem \[Tul09, Theorem 5.3\], there are constants _C_<sub>0</sub>_,c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 and graphs on arbitrarily large numbers _N_ of vertices for which the independent-set relaxation after \(L_N:=\lfloor 2^{c_0q_N}\rfloor\) rounds has a feasible vector solution of value

\(B\ge\frac{\alpha(G)N}{2^s},s:=C_0q_N.\) (19)

Adjusting the constants accounts for the choice of logarithm base and for integer rounding. We first convert the vector solution into a pseudo-distribution, retaining half the original number of rounds, rounded down.

In Tulsiani’s formulation, the vectors _u<sub>A</sub>_ are indexed by subsets \(A\subseteq V\) of size at most _L<sub>N</sub>_. They satisfy \(\|u_\emptyset\|=1\), the edge constraints \(\langle u_{\{v\}},u_{\{w\}}\rangle=0\) for \(\{v,w\}\in E\), and the consistency constraints

\(\langle u_A,u_B\rangle=\langle u_C,u_D\rangle\text{whenever}A\cup B=C\cup D.\)

Each of the four sets must index an available vector. The objective is \(B=\sum_{v\in V}\|u_{\{v\}}\|^2\).

<tbc>Set \(m:=\lfloor L_N/2\rfloor\), and take _N_ sufficiently large that \(m\ge 1\). For every \(Q\subseteq V\) with \(|Q|\le 2m\), define<tbc>

\(\mu(Q):=\langle u_Q,u_\emptyset\rangle.\)

<tbc>The required vectors are available because \(2m\le L_N\). Normalization gives \(\mu(\emptyset)=1\). For \(|A|,|B|\le m\), consistency gives

\(\mu(A\cup B)=\langle u_{A\cup B},u_\emptyset\rangle=\langle u_A,u_B\rangle.\)

The first step follows from the definition of \(\mu\), and the second step follows from consistency. Thus the level-_m_ moment matrix is the Gram matrix of the vectors _u<sub>A</sub>_ with \(|A|\le m\) and is therefore positive semidefinite.

It remains to verify that the moments of sets containing an edge vanish. Let \(e=\{v,w\}\in E\). Consistency and the edge constraint give<tbc>

\(\|u_e\|^2=\langle u_{\{v\}},u_{\{w\}}\rangle=0.\)

<tbc>The first step follows from consistency, and the second step follows from the edge constraint. Hence _u<sub>e</sub>_=0. If \(e\subseteq Q\) and \(|Q|\le 2m\), consistency again gives

\(\mu(Q)=\langle u_Q,u_\emptyset\rangle=\langle u_Q,u_e\rangle=0.\)

The first step follows from the definition of \(\mu\), the second step follows from consistency and \(Q\cup e=Q\), and the third step uses _u<sub>e</sub>_=0. Therefore \(\mu\) is a level-_m_ pseudo-distribution. Its objective is preserved: for each _v_, we have \(\mu(v)=\langle u_{\{v\}},u_\emptyset\rangle=\|u_{\{v\}}\|^2\). The first step follows from the definition of \(\mu\), and the second step follows from consistency. Summing over _v_ gives the objective _B_.

Choose _c_:=_c_<sub>0</sub>/2. Integer rounding gives \(m\ge 2^{c_0q_N}/2-1\). For all sufficiently large _N_, this lower bound is at least 2<sup>_c_<sub>0</sub>_q<sub>N</sub>/_2</sup>, because \(q_N\rightarrow\infty\). After discarding finitely many graph sizes, we may therefore assume \(m\ge\lfloor 2^{cq_N}\rfloor=R_N\). Restricting \(\mu\) to any level \(1\le r\le R_N\) preserves its objective, and hence

\(\mathrm{Las}_r(G)\ge B\ge\alpha(G)N2^{-s}.\)

The first step follows because restriction preserves feasibility and the objective; the second step follows from Eq. (19). Also \(B\le N\), because each singleton marginal of a feasible pseudo-distribution is at most 1. Combining this with Eq. (19) gives \(\alpha(G)\le 2^s\).

Take \(T:=\lfloor s\rfloor+1\) and _C_:=_C_<sub>0</sub>+1. Since \(N\ge 4\) implies \(q_N\ge 1\), we have<tbc>

\(1\le T\le s+1\le Cq_N.\)

<tbc>The first step follows from _s\>_0, the second step uses \(\lfloor s\rfloor\le s\), and the third step uses _s=C_<sub>0</sub>_q<sub>N</sub>_ and \(q_N\ge 1\). Since \(N\ge 4\), we have \(\alpha(G)\ge 1\). Therefore, for every \(1\le r\le R_N\),

\(\mathrm{Las}_r(G)\ge\alpha(G)N2^{-s}\ge N2^{-s}>N2^{-T},\alpha(G)\le 2^s<2^T.\)

In the first chain, the first step follows from the objective bound above, the second step uses \(\alpha(G)\ge 1\), and the third step uses _T\>s_. In the second chain, the first step follows by combining \(B\le N\) with Eq. (19), and the second step uses _T\>s_. This proves Eq. (18).

To state the consequence precisely, let \(t_\mathrm{max}(N)\ge 1\) and \(r(N,t)\ge 1\) be integer-valued functions. Suppose that, for every \(N\ge 4\), every graph _G_ on _N_ vertices and every integer \(1\le t\le t_\mathrm{max}(N)\), one has<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Las}_{r(N,t)}(G)\ge 2^{-t}N\Longrightarrow\alpha(G)\ge 2^t.\)

<tbc>Assume that the number of levels is subexponential in _q<sub>N</sub>_, uniformly over this parameter range, in the precise sense that<tbc>

\(max_{1\le t\le t_{max}(N)}logr(N,t)=o(q_N)\text{as}N\rightarrow\infty.\)

<tbc>For all sufficiently large _N_, every such level is at most _R<sub>N</sub>_. For each sufficiently large graph size supplied by Proposition 4.8, the associated integer _T_ must therefore satisfy \(t_{max}(N)<T\le Cq_N\): otherwise the proposed implication at _t=T_ contradicts Eq. (18). This bounds the valid parameter range for infinitely many values of _N_. In particular, it rules out a universal range \(t_{max}(N)=\omega(\sqrt{logNloglogN})\) under the stated level bound. For any fixed _a\>_0 and \(\beta>1/2\), one has

\(\frac{a(logN)^\beta}{q_N}=\frac{a(logN)^{\beta-1/2}}{\sqrt{loglogN}}\longrightarrow\infty.\)

The first step uses the definition of _q<sub>N</sub>_, and the second step follows because a positive power of log_N_ grows faster than \(\sqrt{loglogN}\). Hence a universal range \(t_{max}(N)\ge a(logN)^\beta\) for all sufficiently large _N_ is impossible under the stated level bound. This is a restriction on this implication from the Lasserre value and does not exclude algorithms using additional properties of the graph.
